report:
## Conclusion

Probiotics appear to produce a **modest, generally beneficial but inconsistent effect** on blood sugar in type 2 diabetes. Multiple meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials find that probiotic (and synbiotic) supplementation, on average, lowers fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), and sometimes HbA1c compared with placebo, particularly in people with poorly controlled diabetes and those not on insulin therapy (Advances in Nutrition, https://advances.nutrition.org/article/S2161-8313(22)00101-6/fulltext). A large systematic review/meta-analysis in *Diabetologia* similarly reported significant reductions in fasting glucose and insulin, though HbA1c improvement was smaller and not statistically significant overall (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00125-020-05295-1).

However, individual trials are mixed: some newer randomized controlled trials found **no significant difference in HbA1c or fasting glucose** between probiotic and placebo groups (ScienceDirect trial, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2405457725003109), and effects vary widely by probiotic strain, dose, and treatment duration (PMC, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11303337/). Proposed mechanisms include gut microbiota production of short-chain fatty acids, improved GLP-1 secretion, and reduced inflammation/endotoxemia, but confirmation in humans is incomplete.

**Bottom line:** Current evidence suggests probiotics can modestly improve some glycemic markers (fasting glucose, insulin resistance) in type 2 diabetes, but effects on HbA1c are inconsistent and generally small. Probiotics should be seen as a possible adjunct—not a replacement—for standard diabetes treatment, and further high-quality, strain-specific trials are needed.
